Build coverage clauses once and use MiniCard’s native cardinality constraint for each bound. This avoids repeatedly encoding a sequential counter CNF during binary search, reducing formula construction and SAT overhead while preserving exact minimum-set-cover semantics.

Build coverage clauses in linear input size, use a greedy feasible cover as the initial upper bound, and avoid quadratic model-membership checks. The greedy bound preserves optimality because it only narrows the search to a known-feasible solution size.

Collapse identical non-empty subsets before SAT encoding. Duplicate sets never improve an unweighted set-cover solution, so this reduces SAT variables, cardinality constraints, and greedy candidates while retaining the first original index for the returned solution.

Compute the cardinality lower bound from the original universe before greedy cover construction. The current expression uses `uncovered` after greedy selection, when it is always empty, so SAT unnecessarily tests infeasible small cover sizes. The universe-size bound is valid because each selected subset can cover at most `max_subset_size` elements.

Replace repeated full set intersections in the greedy upper-bound construction with lazy heap updates driven by newly covered elements. This reduces greedy initialization cost substantially on dense instances. Preserve the original universe size before coverage is consumed, so the cardinality lower bound is valid rather than always collapsing to one.

Reuse one SAT instance across the binary search and encode the cardinality bound once with an incremental totalizer. This avoids repeatedly constructing and initializing a MiniCard solver with identical coverage clauses, while assumptions cheaply test each candidate bound. The returned model is interpreted exactly as before.
Build the cardinality encoding once and reuse one SAT solver across the binary search. Assumption-based bounds avoid repeatedly constructing identical coverage solvers and cardinality constraints.

Kernelize sets that are logically mandatory: if an element appears in exactly one subset, that subset must occur in every feasible cover. Remove all elements covered by these forced subsets and solve only the remaining residual instance. This reduces SAT variables, coverage clauses, greedy work, and cardinality-search bounds without changing the optimal result.

Preserve the maximum residual subset gain before greedy selection mutates all gains to zero. This yields a valid, tighter cardinality lower bound for the SAT optimization phase, often avoiding several satisfiability calls without changing solution correctness.

Remove every subset that is strictly contained in another available subset before building the SAT instance. A dominated subset can never be required in a minimum-cardinality cover: replacing it with its superset preserves coverage without increasing the number of selected sets. This reduces both greedy-heap work and the number of SAT variables/clauses while preserving correctness.

Remove non-forced subsets whose remaining uncovered elements are a strict subset of another available subset’s remaining coverage. With unit-cost sets, a dominating superset is always at least as good, reducing greedy-heap work and SAT variables while preserving the optimum.

Remove equivalent residual subsets, remap SAT variables to a dense range, and derive a safe packing lower bound. This reduces solver memory/encoding size and can eliminate unnecessary SAT searches while preserving the exact optimum.

Break equal-gain greedy ties toward subsets covering rarer elements, producing tighter feasible upper bounds. Strengthen the SAT lower bound by taking the best of two valid, deterministic disjoint-choice packings over only eligible subsets; each packed element requires a distinct selected subset.
